results.summary: This design is a multi-tool system-on-chip that implements a small alphabet-driven operating system with hardware engines for Euclidean greatest common divisor, integer square root, and a cryptographic linear-feedback shift register. It is controlled through the Tiny Tapeout demo board's DIP switches and 7-segment display, using a debounced enter switch to step through opcode, operand, and result states. The 8-bit result is shown by multiplexing the hundreds, tens, and units digits on the display, with the decimal point marking the most significant digit. A test mode pin can bypass the internal timers for faster operation at low clock speeds.

This design implements eight parallel glitch detectors intended to detect loss of setup and hold margin in the system clock domain, inspired by the Raspberry RP2350 security peripheral. Each detector uses a pair of flip-flops with a programmable delay line in one feedback path, and a mismatch between the flip-flops latches a trigger output. The detectors have different sensitivities, with delay chains parametrized between 70% and 140% of the 25 MHz clock period. Testing requires external fault-injection equipment such as a ChipWhisperer or ChipSHOUTER, and the design is explicitly experimental and untested.

The project is described as a potential processor but currently only implements an arithmetic logic unit. The pin names suggest a 4-bit nibble input, a 4-bit address input, an 8-bit bidirectional port, and an 8-bit output, but the documentation refers only to a file 'tapeout.typ' for details. No functional description, test procedure, or external hardware requirements are provided in the available text. The design is essentially undocumented beyond its title and pin names.

This project has no meaningful documentation: the one-line description is 'tbd', the how-it-works and how-to-test sections are placeholders, and the external hardware section is a template. The pin names indicate two inputs and one output, but their function is not described. It is impossible to determine what the design does or how to use it from the provided information. The project appears to be an early-stage or abandoned submission.

This design is a sequential neural network inference accelerator for the MNIST dataset, featuring an 8-bit multiply-accumulate datapath and an 11-state control finite state machine. It is intended to be driven by an external microcontroller such as the RP2040 or RP2350 on the Tiny Tapeout demo board, which feeds pre-trained weights and input data through the 8-bit input pins while controlling data type and toggling. The chip outputs a 4-bit classification result for one of ten digit classes, along with status signals such as busy, done, and error flag. The design occupies a 1x2 tile area and runs at 50 MHz.

This design attempts to recreate the Chrome dinosaur jumping game, outputting a VGA signal with 2-bit color per channel plus sync signals. The game is controlled by a single button connected to input index 1, which makes the character jump. The documentation is minimal and does not describe the game mechanics, scoring, or any limitations beyond the admission that the attempt 'failed'. No external hardware beyond a VGA display and a button is mentioned.

This is a purely combinational 8-bit prime number detector that uses a 256-bit lookup table to identify primes from 0 to 255. The lower hex nibble of the input number is displayed on the 7-segment display, and the decimal point lights up when the number is prime. It requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout demo board's DIP switches and 7-segment display. The design is notable for its zero-latency operation and minimal gate count of about 100 gates.

This analog tile contains three operational amplifier test circuits: an inverting amplifier with external feedback, a voltage follower, and an R2R digital-to-analog converter. It also includes auxiliary circuits such as a PTAT current source, resistor divider, level shifters, and a decoder. The design uses three analog pins for a 3.3 V supply, op-amp output, and input signal, and is controlled via digital pins for DAC input and circuit selection. Testing requires external equipment including DIP switches, LED PMOD, a 3.3 V supply, a function generator, and an oscilloscope or multimeter.

This design is a ring oscillator built from a chain of 21 SkullFET inverters, producing a square wave output with an expected frequency of about 150.5 MHz. It provides divided outputs at 75.3 MHz, 37.6 MHz, and 18.8 MHz. The circuit is intended to be tested by connecting an oscilloscope to one of the output pins. The design is notable for its use of SkullFET transistors and its stylish theme.

This design is a fault injection pulse generator with configurable parameters, controllable over UART. It implements a state machine with idle, target reset, delay, pulse active, and pulse spacing phases, and provides outputs for pulse, target reset, busy, armed, and a combined pulse-or-reset signal. The trigger input is synchronized and active high, with a minimum trigger-to-pulse latency of 60-80 ns. External hardware such as a MOSFET, analog switch, or ChipSHOUTER is required to perform voltage or electromagnetic fault injection.
